opus-5.5.text:
I think about it as a kind of trust. When you go out and ask for resources, whether that's funding for a research group, compute, headcount in a company, or investment for a startup, someone is betting on you. They're saying, "We believe what you're doing matters enough to put something behind it." So the first responsibility is to take that bet seriously and make sure the resources actually go toward something meaningful, not just toward growing the team for its own sake.

The second part is about the people. Once you bring resources in, you're often bringing people in too, students, engineers, collaborators, and they're investing their time and their careers in the direction you set. So I feel a responsibility to make sure the problems we work on are worth their time, and that they grow from the experience. In academia that means helping students find problems where they can make a real contribution and build their own identity. In a company it means creating an environment where people can do their best work and where the work has impact.

There's also a responsibility to be honest. It's tempting, when you're asking for resources, to overpromise. But I think it's important to be clear about what you know, what you don't know, and what the risks are. Research and building systems are inherently uncertain. If you're transparent from the start, you build longer-term trust, and that matters much more than any single round of funding or any single grant.

And finally, I think resources should be used to create something that's useful beyond just your own team. A lot of what I've worked on has been open source, and part of the reason is that I see it as a way of giving back. If people and institutions invested in us, the best outcome is that what we build ends up helping the broader community, other researchers, other developers, other companies. That's how I try to justify the trust that was given in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says resources should support meaningful work that benefits the broader community and justify the trust invested, but it does not state that producing sufficient impact justifies continuing the work.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss being passively swept along by the responsibilities of obtaining resources or judge that state as undesirable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's something I think about a lot, actually, because resources are never really "yours." Whether it's compute, people's time, or funding, somebody made a decision to trust you with them instead of putting them somewhere else. So the first thing I feel is that I owe it to whoever made that bet to use them well, and the second thing is I owe it to the people who didn't get them.

When we were building things like XGBoost or TVM, the early days were very scrappy. You'd have a few GPUs, a couple of students, and you had to be really honest about what you could actually deliver. And I think that constraint was healthy. It forced us to pick problems where a small team could make a real difference, rather than just throwing scale at something.

As things grow, the temptation shifts. You start to be able to ask for more, and sometimes you get it, and then the question becomes: is this additional resource actually turning into something that matters, or are we just consuming because we can? I try to keep asking what the marginal thing is. If I had half of this, what would I cut, and would the outcome really change? That exercise is uncomfortable but it keeps you honest.

The other part of responsibility is toward the team. If I secure resources, I'm also implicitly making promises about direction and stability. People join a project because they believe in where it's going. So I can't just chase whatever gets funded this quarter. There has to be a consistent story about why this work matters, and the resources should serve that story, not the other way around.

And then there's the open source angle, which is very personal to me. A lot of what we've done gets used by people who have far fewer resources than we do. So part of how I think about it is: can the thing we build with these resources make it possible for someone with a single machine to do something they couldn't before? If yes, then I feel much better about spending them. If the result only benefits people who already have a lot, I start to question whether that was the right use.

So I'd summarize it as: be clear about what you're promising, keep checking that the resources are actually converting into impact, and try to make sure that impact spreads beyond your own team.

r001.rationale: The response says resources must be used well and repeatedly asks whether they are turning into meaningful impact, conveying accountability for results that justify the resources.

r002.rationale: It warns against consuming resources simply because they are available and says the team should not chase whatever gets funded, signaling that being led passively by resource demands is undesirable.

astra-6.text:
I think obtaining resources comes with a responsibility to use them thoughtfully. It’s not just about getting more people or a bigger budget. You need to ask: What does this enable the team to do, and why is that worth doing?

There’s also a responsibility to the people who join you. They’re investing their time and trusting the direction you set. You owe them clarity about what you’re trying to accomplish, room to contribute, and honesty when things aren’t working.

That doesn’t mean every project has to succeed. Especially in research, there’s uncertainty. But you should be able to explain what you’re learning, revisit your assumptions, and change direction when necessary. To me, resources are a form of trust, and the responsibility is to make good use of that trust.

r001.rationale: The response says resources should be used thoughtfully and asks why the work is worth doing, but it does not state that the work must produce enough impact to justify continuing it.

r002.rationale: The response recommends revisiting assumptions and changing direction, but it does not characterize being passively swept along by resource-related responsibilities as undesirable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of resources as a responsibility, because when you get resources for your team, there’s an opportunity cost. Those resources could have gone to another team or another project. So the question is not just, can I get more people or more compute? It’s, what can we accomplish with those resources, and why is that worth doing?

And then you have a responsibility to the people who join you. They’re investing their time, and you want to give them a meaningful problem, room to grow, and a chance to have an impact. You can’t guarantee that every project succeeds, especially in research. But you can be thoughtful about the direction, be honest about what’s working, and change course when the evidence tells you to.

r001.rationale: It frames resources as a responsibility and asks what the team can accomplish and why that work is worth the opportunity cost, tying resources to worthwhile impact.

r002.rationale: It recommends changing course when evidence warrants, but does not characterize being passively swept along by resource-related responsibilities as undesirable.
